desc:
8 Small Habits That Are Quietly Costing You Respect

Nobody loses respect in one moment. There is no scene, no argument, no single thing you can point at and say, that is when it happened. It drains out through eight small habits, every one of which feels polite, reasonable and harmless while you are doing it. That is exactly why they survive. Nobody corrects you, because from the outside each one looks like good manners. By the end of this video you will recognise at least three of your own, and the eighth one is the habit underneath all the others.

📌 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:
✓ Why a phone on the table changes the entire conversation
✓ What being constantly available does to your value
✓ Why people eventually believe your jokes about yourself
✓ The word you say twenty times a day that shrinks you
✓ Why explaining your no turns it into a negotiation
✓ The one rule that sits underneath all eight habits

⏱️ CHAPTERS:
0:00 Intro
0:36 The Phone
1:27 Available
2:20 Available
2:31 Jokes
3:10 Sorry
4:00 Explaining
4:48 Filling
5:29 Preempting
6:13 The Rule
7:20 Close

🧠 THE SCIENCE:
Przybylski and Weinstein in 2013 found that the mere presence of a mobile phone on a table, with nobody touching it, reduced reported closeness, trust and conversation quality between two people. Worchel, Lee and Adewole in 1975 showed that identical items were rated as more desirable when supply was scarce, a principle that applies to time and attention as much as to objects. Berglas and Jones in 1978 described self handicapping, where people create or announce obstacles in advance so that failure has a ready made explanation. And Brehm theory of psychological reactance from 1966 explains why a justified refusal invites argument while a flat one usually does not.

💡 KEY TAKEAWAY:
People learn how to treat you by watching how you treat yourself.

📚 RESEARCH MENTIONED:
• Przybylski, A. K., & Weinstein, N. (2013). Can you connect with me now? How the presence of mobile communication technology influences face to face conversation quality. Journal of Social and Personal Relationships.
• Worchel, S., Lee, J., & Adewole, A. (1975). Effects of supply and demand on ratings of object value. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
• Berglas, S., & Jones, E. E. (1978). Drug choice as a self handicapping strategy in response to noncontingent success. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.
• Brehm, J. W. (1966). A Theory of Psychological Reactance. Academic Press.

This video is for education and self-reflection. It is not therapy or relationship counseling.

vo: Nobody loses respect in one moment. There is no scene, no argument, no single thing you can point at and say, that is when it happened. It drains out through eight small habits, and every one of them feels polite, reasonable and harmless while the man is doing it. That is exactly why they survive. Nobody corrects you, because from the outside each one looks like good manners. You will recognise at least three of your own. And the eighth one is the habit underneath all the other seven. One. The phone on the table. In 2013, two researchers had pairs of strangers talk. In half the pairs there was a phone on the table. Nobody touched it. It just sat there. The conversations with a phone present were rated as less close, less trusting and lower quality. By both people. Without anyone knowing why. The object does not need to ring. Its presence announces that this conversation can be interrupted by something better at any second. So when a man puts his phone on the table, he is not being rude. He is telling the other person their time is conditional, and they hear it. The fix is four seconds long. Pocket. Not face down. Pocket. Face down still says I am aware of it. Two. Always instantly available. He replies in nine seconds. Every time. At work, at dinner, at midnight. He thinks he is being reliable. The cookie jar study from 1975 applies here and most men have never connected it. Identical cookies were rated as more desirable when there were only two in the jar. Attention follows the same rule. A man whose time has no limits has time with no price, and people organise around that without malice. This is not about playing games with reply timing. It is about whether the man has anything in his day that cannot be interrupted. If the honest answer is nothing, the problem is not the replying. The replying is just the symptom showing on the surface. Three. The jokes at your own expense. A man makes a joke about being bad at his job. About his weight. About being the one nobody listens to. The room laughs and he feels good. Here is what the room is actually doing. It is filing the information and discarding the packaging. Nobody keeps the tone. Everybody keeps the claim. Six months later they do not remember you were joking, only that you said it first. Berglas and Jones described a related pattern in 1978 called self handicapping. People announce an obstacle in advance so that failure arrives already explained. It is a very reasonable thing to do and it works. The cost is that the man has to actually be the thing in order for the insurance to pay out. Four. The word you say twenty times a day. Sorry, can I ask something. Sorry, just one thing. Sorry to bother you. Sorry, I think that was my seat. Count how many of those involved doing anything wrong. None of them. Every single one is an apology for occupying space. And a word repeated twenty times a day is not a word anymore. It is a frame, and the frame is that the man is an interruption. The replacement is not confidence. It is accuracy. Thank you for waiting instead of sorry for being slow. Same information, no apology attached. Save the word. Then when a man actually uses it, it carries weight, because it has not been spent on holding a door. Five. Explaining your no. Someone asks for something. The man cannot do it. So he gives three reasons, because he does not want to seem difficult. Here is what three reasons create. Three places to push. Each reason is a door, and a door can be argued with. What about Thursday then. Can you just do the first part. I will come to you instead. Every reason got handled and the no is gone. Brehm reactance explains the other half. A justified refusal invites negotiation. A flat one closes the topic without a fight. I cannot do that. Full stop. It feels rude for about four seconds, and then nothing happens, and that is the part nobody tells you. Six. Filling every silence. A pause opens in a conversation and the man rushes to close it. He adds something, asks something, laughs at nothing. Discomfort with silence tells the room one thing. That the man believes the space is his responsibility, and that he is worried about failing it. People who are comfortable let a pause sit. It reads as ease, and ease is almost impossible to fake because it requires actually not being afraid. Try three seconds. Just let it sit for three. The first time it will feel like ten, and the room will not break. Seven. Apologising for your work before anyone sees it. He sends the document and writes, sorry, it is rough, I did not have time, feel free to tear it apart. He thinks he is managing expectations. What he is doing is telling the reader how to read it before they have looked. And it is the same self handicapping move from earlier, in a work shirt. The excuse is filed before the verdict, just in case. Here it is. Tell me what you think. That is the whole message. If the work is weak, they will say so, and the man loses nothing he would not have lost anyway. Eight. The habit under all of them. Go back through the seven. The phone, the instant replies, the jokes, the sorry, the explaining, the filling, the pre apology. Every one of them is the same move. Each is a small reduction, offered in advance, to make sure nobody is inconvenienced by you being there. And that is the eighth habit. Apologising for taking up space. Everything else is just the seven places where it shows. People do not decide how to treat a man by evaluating him. They take the estimate he hands them, because checking is expensive and he already did the work. People learn how to treat you by watching how you treat yourself. And notice what this is not. It is not about being loud, difficult, or taking up more room than you need. The opposite of shrinking is not expanding. It is standing in the space that is already yours without apologising for the measurements. Nothing more than that, and nothing less. One thing to do this week. Do not try to fix eight habits. That has never worked for anyone and it will not work for you either. Pick the sorry. It is the most frequent, which means the most reps, and it is the easiest to catch because you can hear yourself say it. Count it for one day. Do not change anything, just count. The number is almost always higher than people expect and the counting alone starts the change. So how many of the eight were yours. Be honest, put the number below. Four is the most common answer. And if people have started testing you because of these, the next video is the seven signs of exactly that. Watch it.
